identity.name: Buoyancy - hydrostatic balance with magnetic suspension - two sinkers
identity.thermoml_standard_name: Buoyancy - hydrostatic balance with magnetic suspension - two sinkers

direct_observables: apparent weight of sinker 1 in vacuum (W1_vac) via magnetic suspension balance
apparent weight of sinker 1 immersed in sample fluid (W1_fluid)
apparent weight of sinker 2 in vacuum (W2_vac) via magnetic suspension balance
apparent weight of sinker 2 immersed in sample fluid (W2_fluid)
differential apparent weight ΔW_diff = (W1_vac − W1_fluid) − (W2_vac − W2_fluid), proportional to differential buoyancy
coupling/decoupling positions of the magnetic suspension for each sinker (zero-point, measuring-point-sinker-1, measuring-point-sinker-2)
temperature of the measuring cell (via calibrated PRT)
pressure of the measuring cell (via calibrated transducer)
derived_observables: fluid density ρ = [(W1_vac − W1_fluid) − (W2_vac − W2_fluid)] / [(V1(T,p) − V2(T,p)) · g], the primary derived quantity from differential weighing
excess molar volume V^E for binary or multicomponent mixtures
isothermal compressibility κ_T = (1/ρ)(∂ρ/∂p)_T from ρ(p) isotherms
isobaric thermal expansion coefficient α_p = −(1/ρ)(∂ρ/∂T)_p from ρ(T) isobars
speed of sound (when combined with Cp data via thermodynamic relation)
target_properties: liquid density (compressed and saturated liquid) with sub-0.01 kg/m³ uncertainty
gas and vapor density at moderate to high pressures
isobaric thermal expansion coefficient (derived from ρ(T) isobars)
supported_sample_types: pure liquids (organic solvents, refrigerants, hydrocarbons, ionic liquids)
pure gases and vapors at sufficient density (typically > 2 kg/m³)
cryogenic liquids (e.g., LNG constituents, liquid noble gases)
natural gas mixtures at pipeline conditions
unsupported_sample_types: solids (sinkers must be freely suspended in a fluid)
highly viscous fluids (> ~10 Pa·s) — viscous drag on sinkers and slow equilibration distort buoyancy readings
strongly corrosive fluids that attack sinker or cell materials unless specialized alloy sinkers are used
very low-density gases at low pressures (differential buoyancy force too small to resolve)
slurries or suspensions containing particles that could adsorb onto sinkers or interfere with magnetic coupling
magnetic fluids (ferrofluids) — interfere with the magnetic suspension mechanism
multiphase systems where the two sinkers may reside in different phases
typical_output_formats: ρ(T, p) tables at discrete temperature and pressure state points
ρ vs. T isobars (density as a function of temperature at constant pressure)
ρ vs. p isotherms (density as a function of pressure at constant temperature)
fitted equation of state parameters (e.g., modified Tait, MBWR, or Helmholtz energy formulation coefficients)
deviation plots: (ρ_exp − ρ_EOS)/ρ_EOS vs. T or p

constraints.hard_limits: lower limit ~90 K with cryogenic cooling; upper limit ~573 K limited by magnetic coupling stability, seal materials, and sinker material properties; PTB and NIST instruments have operated to 520 K
constraints.notes: temperature stability of ±2 mK or better is required to achieve the full potential of the two-sinker technique; thermostat performance is typically the limiting factor at extreme temperatures

constraints.hard_limits: maximum ~200 MPa for specialized high-pressure cells (e.g., Ruhr-Universität Bochum instruments); some designs reach 300 MPa; minimum pressure limited by adequate differential buoyancy force
constraints.notes: cell material (stainless steel, Hastelloy C-276, titanium, or sapphire windows) determines the pressure ceiling; the two-sinker differential cancellation of FTE is most beneficial at extreme pressures where single-sinker FTE corrections become large

constraints.typical_range: sinker 1: 10–30 cm³; sinker 2: 3–15 cm³ (must differ significantly in volume)
constraints.hard_limits: the volume difference (V1 − V2) must be large enough to generate a resolvable differential buoyancy signal for the target fluid density; typical volume ratios V1/V2 range from 2:1 to 5:1
constraints.notes: sinker 1 is typically a low-density material (quartz glass, ~2.2 g/cm³) with large volume; sinker 2 is a high-density material (silicon, titanium, or gold-plated stainless steel) with smaller volume but similar mass, maximizing the volume difference while keeping both within the balance capacity

constraints.typical_range: 100 cm³ to 400 cm³ (measuring cell must accommodate both sinkers)
constraints.hard_limits: cell must be large enough for both sinkers to be weighed sequentially without wall proximity effects; adequate clearance on all sides of each sinker is essential
constraints.notes: the two-sinker method inherently requires a larger cell than the one-sinker method; for mixture measurements the entire cell volume must be homogeneous

constraints.hard_limits: balance resolution must resolve the differential buoyancy force; however, because FTE cancels in the two-sinker method, the absolute accuracy requirement on the balance is relaxed compared to the one-sinker method
constraints.notes: microbalance zero-point stability is less critical than in the one-sinker technique because the differential measurement cancels common-mode drifts

variables.name: temperature
variables.typical_values: 233 K to 523 K, scanned in steps of 5–20 K for isobaric surveys; finer steps (0.5–2 K) near phase boundaries or in critical region
variables.effect: density decreases with increasing temperature at constant pressure; thermal expansion is mapped by measuring ρ(T) isobars

variables.name: pressure
variables.typical_values: 0.1 MPa to 100 MPa, in steps of 1–10 MPa for isothermal surveys
variables.effect: density increases with increasing pressure at constant temperature; pressure dependence yields compressibility information

variables.name: composition
variables.typical_values: full mole fraction range, typically in steps of 0.05–0.20
variables.effect: excess molar volume and mixing density are mapped as a function of mixture composition

variables.name: coupling_position
variables.typical_values: zero-point (both sinkers on cradle), measuring-point-1 (sinker 1 lifted), measuring-point-2 (sinker 2 lifted)
variables.effect: the three-position coupling mechanism sequentially weighs each sinker and records a zero-point; the two sinker weighings are performed at the same coupling/decoupling position so that FTE cancels in the difference

instrument_components: magnetic suspension coupling — electromagnetically controlled suspension magnet inside the pressurized cell, coupled through a non-magnetic cell wall to a permanent magnet attached to the balance weighing hook; the coupling has at least three stable positions: zero-point (both sinkers resting on cradles), measuring-position-1 (sinker 1 lifted to weighing position), and measuring-position-2 (sinker 2 lifted to weighing position)

analytical microbalance — high-resolution balance (readability 1–10 μg, capacity 50–250 g) mounted above the pressure cell; measures the apparent weight transmitted through the magnetic coupling for each sinker sequentially
sinker 1 (large volume, low density) — typically quartz glass, volume ~15–30 cm³, mass ~30–70 g, polished surface; provides the larger buoyancy signal due to greater displaced fluid volume

sinker 2 (small volume, high density) — typically silicon single crystal, titanium, or gold-plated stainless steel, volume ~4–12 cm³, mass ~20–60 g; chosen so that m1 ≈ m2 but V1 >> V2 to maximize the differential volume (V1 − V2)
sinker support cradles — individual resting positions inside the cell for each sinker when not being weighed; designed so that the coupling mechanism can selectively lift one sinker at a time

pressurized measuring cell — thick-walled vessel (stainless steel 316L, Hastelloy C-276, or titanium alloy) large enough to house both sinkers with adequate clearance; equipped with fluid inlet/outlet ports and temperature sensor ports

thermostat system — high-stability liquid-bath thermostat or multi-zone circulating jacket surrounding the measuring cell, providing temperature stability of ±2 mK or better; secondary radiation shields for high-temperature operation
temperature sensors — calibrated platinum resistance thermometers (Pt-25 or Pt-100) mounted on or embedded in the measuring cell wall; traceable to ITS-90
pressure transducer — high-accuracy pressure sensor (quartz crystal or vibrating cylinder type) with uncertainty ≤ 0.01% of reading; connected to the cell via capillary tubing
pressure generator — automated syringe pump or screw-type piston pump for precise pressure setting and maintenance

control and data acquisition system — computer controlling the thermostat, pressure generator, magnetic coupling sequence, and balance readings; manages the sequential sinker-1/sinker-2/zero-point measurement cycle at each state point
vacuum pump — for initial evacuation of the measuring cell and filling lines
environmental_requirements: temperature-controlled laboratory (±1 K) to minimize thermal drift in balance electronics and magnetic coupling
vibration-isolated support for the balance and cell assembly — the magnetic suspension coupling is sensitive to mechanical disturbances
draft-free enclosure around the balance head to eliminate air convection effects on the weighing
adequate ventilation or fume hood for volatile, toxic, or flammable fluids
electromagnetic shielding to prevent stray magnetic fields from interfering with the suspension coupling

geometry: homogeneous fluid phase — liquid, compressed gas, or supercritical fluid
no geometric constraints on the sample itself; the cell is filled with the fluid surrounding both sinkers
sample_requirements.size_limits: 100–400 cm³ of fluid per filling (larger than one-sinker method due to dual sinker accommodation); some miniaturized designs require ~50 cm³
surface_requirements: fluid must not deposit films, precipitates, or crystals on either sinker surface — such deposits change the effective sinker volume and mass, and would not cancel in the differential measurement
no particulate contamination that could lodge between sinkers, cradles, or the coupling magnet
mounting_requirements: both sinkers are placed inside the measuring cell on their respective cradles before sealing
cell is sealed with high-pressure fittings and o-rings or metal gaskets rated for the target pressure and chemically compatible with the sample
preparation_requirements: degas the sample thoroughly to prevent bubble formation on sinker surfaces, which would not cancel in differential measurement if bubbles attach preferentially to one sinker
for mixtures, prepare gravimetrically with verified composition (weighed on an analytical balance, uncertainty < 0.01 mol%)
filter samples through sub-micron filters to remove particulate matter
dry hygroscopic samples or handle under inert atmosphere to prevent moisture uptake
verify sample purity by GC, Karl Fischer titration, or other appropriate analytical method

calibration_requirements: sinker volume calibration: determine V1(T,p) and V2(T,p) independently by measuring each sinker's buoyancy in reference fluids of precisely known density (water via IAPWS-95; nitrogen via Span et al. EOS) at multiple T, p state points; fit thermal expansion and compressibility coefficients for each sinker material

sinker mass calibration: weigh each sinker in vacuum against SI-traceable mass standards; the two-sinker method requires knowledge of (m1 − m2) but the differential approach relaxes the absolute accuracy needed for individual masses

differential force transmission error verification: although the two-sinker method cancels FTE to first order, verify this cancellation by performing differential measurements in vacuum — the residual should be indistinguishable from zero within balance noise
balance calibration: verify linearity and span using certified mass standards
temperature sensor calibration: calibrate PRTs against ITS-90 fixed points or a reference-standard PRT
pressure transducer calibration: calibrate against a dead-weight pressure gauge traceable to a national metrology institute
reference_materials: ultrapure water — IAPWS-95 equation of state provides density to < 0.001 kg/m³ over wide T, p range; primary calibration and validation fluid
nitrogen gas — reference equation of state (Span et al. 2000) for gas-phase calibration of sinker volumes
silicon single crystal — density known to < 0.01 kg/m³ from X-ray crystal density measurements; used as sinker material with precisely known elastic properties
quartz glass — well-characterized thermal expansion and compressibility; commonly used as the large-volume sinker material
propane, toluene, or n-heptane — secondary liquid reference fluids with high-accuracy reference equations of state for cross-validation
consumables: high-purity sample fluid (sufficient volume to fill and flush the larger two-sinker cell multiple times)
o-rings and seals rated for the operating T, p range and compatible with the sample fluid (FFKM, Viton, PTFE, or metal gaskets)
cleaning solvents (acetone, ethanol, n-hexane) for flushing the cell, both sinkers, and cradles between samples
nitrogen or helium gas for purging and leak testing
safety_notes: high-pressure systems: all pressure vessels and tubing must be rated and tested to at least 1.5× the maximum operating pressure; burst discs or pressure relief valves are mandatory
toxic or flammable fluid handling requires appropriate ventilation, gas detection, and fire suppression
cryogenic operation requires cryogen handling precautions
sinkers (especially the quartz-glass sinker) are fragile and expensive; handle with care during loading to avoid chipping or cracking

performance.sensitivity: density resolution of ~0.001 kg/m³ achievable with optimized sinker volume difference (ΔV ≈ 15–20 cm³) and 10 μg balance readability; the differential technique approximately doubles resolution compared to the one-sinker method for the same balance
performance.detection_limit: minimum measurable fluid density ~1–2 kg/m³; limited by the differential buoyancy force (ΔV · ρ · g) relative to balance resolution; at very low gas densities the differential signal becomes unresolvable

resolution.spatial: not applicable — bulk-averaged density measurement of the homogeneous fluid surrounding both sinkers
resolution.temporal: single state-point measurement requires 10–45 min including thermal and pressure equilibration plus sequential weighing of both sinkers; longer near the critical point

performance.dynamic_range: density from ~2 kg/m³ (dense gas) to ~2000 kg/m³ (heavy liquids, mercury); practical range covers 2–1500 kg/m³ for organic liquids, water, aqueous solutions, and compressed gases
performance.accuracy: 0.001–0.01 kg/m³ for compressed liquids (relative uncertainty ~0.0001–0.001%); 0.01–0.05% for gases and supercritical fluids depending on density level; this is the highest absolute accuracy among all fluid density techniques, rivaling or exceeding single-sinker magnetic suspension methods
performance.precision: 0.001–0.005 kg/m³ (repeatability of replicate measurements at identical T, p); improved over one-sinker due to cancellation of balance drift and FTE in the differential signal
performance.throughput: one sample per cell loading; typically 30–150 state points (T, p) per day for automated scans (slightly slower than one-sinker due to dual weighing cycle); cell cleaning and reloading requires 4–12 hours due to the larger cell and two sinkers
performance.measurement_speed: moderate — each data point takes 10–45 min because both sinkers must be weighed sequentially at each state point; a complete T-p matrix of 100 state points takes 2–5 days of automated operation

data_and_interpretation.raw_signal_type: balance readings (apparent mass in grams or milligrams) at three coupling positions per measurement cycle: zero-point (both sinkers on cradles), sinker-1 lifted (balance reads W1 + coupling force), sinker-2 lifted (balance reads W2 + coupling force); the differential signal eliminates the coupling force and balance offset
preprocessing_steps: zero-point correction: subtract the balance reading at the zero-point position from each sinker weighing to remove tare and drift

differential calculation: compute the difference (W1_vac − W1_fluid) − (W2_vac − W2_fluid) to cancel force transmission error (FTE), balance zero-point drift, and air-side buoyancy effects that are common to both weighings

sinker volume correction: compute V1(T,p) and V2(T,p) at the measurement temperature and pressure using the calibrated thermal expansion and compressibility coefficients of each sinker material; compute ΔV = V1 − V2
temperature and pressure averaging: average the T and p readings recorded during the stable measurement interval and assign them to the density data point

residual FTE correction: although the two-sinker method cancels FTE to first order, a small second-order residual may remain if the sinkers are not at exactly the same levitation position; this is typically negligible (< 1 μg) but can be characterized and corrected if needed
analysis_methods: differential Archimedes relation: ρ_fluid = [(W1_vac − W1_fluid) − (W2_vac − W2_fluid)] / [(V1(T,p) − V2(T,p)) · g_local], the defining equation of the two-sinker method

equation of state fitting: ρ(T, p) data are fitted to a semi-empirical equation (modified Tait, MBWR, Helmholtz energy formulation, or GERG-2008 for natural gas) for interpolation and thermodynamic property derivation
excess volume calculation: V^E = V_mix − Σ(x_i · V_i°) for mixture studies, fitted to Redlich-Kister or NRTL-type models
thermal expansion and compressibility derivation: α_p and κ_T obtained analytically from the fitted ρ(T, p) surface by partial differentiation
consistency checks: compare single-sinker density ρ_1 = (W1_vac − W1_fluid)/(V1 · g) with the differential result to diagnose systematic problems
model_assumptions: the fluid in the measuring cell is homogeneous and in thermodynamic equilibrium at the stated T and p — both sinkers are immersed in fluid of identical density
the sinker volumes V1(T,p) and V2(T,p) are accurately described by their respective calibration models using known thermal expansion and compressibility coefficients
the force transmission error of the magnetic coupling is identical for both sinker weighings (same coupling position) so that it cancels exactly in the differential measurement
gravitational acceleration g is constant and accurately known at the measurement location

fluid adsorption on the two sinker surfaces is either negligible or identical (so that it cancels in the differential weighing); in practice, different sinker materials may adsorb different amounts, introducing a small residual
fit_parameters: fluid density ρ at each (T, p) state point (the primary result)
equation of state parameters (e.g., Tait B, C, ρ_0(T); or Helmholtz energy coefficients) for ρ(T, p) correlation
sinker thermal expansion coefficients α_1, α_2 and isothermal compressibilities κ_1, κ_2 for each sinker material
Redlich-Kister or mixing-rule parameters for excess volume fitting in mixture studies
common_artifacts: differential adsorption artifact: if the two sinkers (e.g., quartz and silicon) adsorb fluid molecules to different extents, the adsorbed mass does NOT cancel in the differential weighing and produces a systematic density bias; this is the primary artifact unique to the two-sinker method and is most significant for polar or associating fluids

bubble nucleation artifact: bubbles forming preferentially on one sinker (due to different surface roughness or wettability) reduce the effective buoyancy asymmetrically, corrupting the differential signal
thermal stratification: if the two sinkers are at different heights in the cell, even a small vertical temperature gradient produces different local densities at each sinker, biasing the result
sinker-sinker interaction: in a small cell, the wake or convection pattern around one sinker can influence the pressure field at the other; adequate sinker separation eliminates this

non-identical coupling positions: if the magnetic coupling does not lift each sinker to exactly the same vertical position relative to the coupling magnet, a residual second-order FTE may remain uncancelled
quality_control_checks: measure the density of a reference fluid (ultrapure water or nitrogen) at multiple T, p points and compare to the IAPWS-95 or Span et al. reference EOS — agreement within 0.003 kg/m³ confirms instrument performance

compare the individual single-sinker densities ρ_1 = ΔW1/(V1·g) and ρ_2 = ΔW2/(V2·g) with the differential result ρ_diff: all three should agree within uncertainty; significant discrepancy indicates FTE or adsorption problems
verify sinker vacuum weights before and after a measurement campaign to detect mass changes from adsorption or corrosion on either sinker
check zero-point reproducibility: repeated coupling/decoupling cycles in vacuum should give consistent balance readings within 5 μg
compare ascending and descending pressure scans at the same temperature (hysteresis check) for evidence of incomplete equilibration or seal leaks
run replicate measurements at selected state points to verify repeatability is within 0.001–0.005 kg/m³
failure_modes: seal failure / leak — loss of sample fluid or ingress of air at high pressure; detected by pressure drop or density anomalies; requires resealing and refilling
sinker touching cell wall or other sinker — if a sinker contacts the inner wall or grazes the other sinker during coupling sequences, the balance reading is corrupted; detected by erratic readings
magnetic coupling loss — excessive vibration or inadequate coupling strength causes a sinker to drop during weighing; detected by sudden balance reading change; requires recoupling
sinker cradle malfunction — if a cradle fails to release a sinker or holds the wrong sinker, the measurement sequence is corrupted; detected by unexpected balance readings at each coupling position
thermostat failure — loss of temperature control invalidates density measurements; detected by temperature sensor readings outside ±5 mK tolerance
pressure transducer failure or drift — incorrect pressure assignment introduces systematic errors in ρ(T, p); detected by cross-check with a secondary gauge
sinker degradation — corrosion or surface deposits on one sinker alter its mass/volume and break the differential cancellation; detected by post-campaign vacuum weighing and visual inspection

uncertainty.level: combined standard uncertainty in density typically 0.001–0.01 kg/m³ (relative: 0.0001–0.001%) for compressed liquids at 0.1–100 MPa and 233–523 K; approximately 2–5× better than the one-sinker method due to cancellation of FTE and balance drift; somewhat larger (0.01–0.1%) for low-density gases and near the critical point
random_sources: balance readout noise and short-term fluctuations during each sinker weighing (~1–10 μg); partially correlated between the two weighings, so cancellation is incomplete
temperature fluctuations from thermostat instability (~1–5 mK), propagating through thermal expansion of fluid, sinker 1, and sinker 2
pressure fluctuations from pump pulsation or regulator instability (~0.001–0.01 MPa)
coupling reproducibility — small random variations in the coupling force; these largely cancel in the differential measurement
vibration-induced noise transmitted to the balance
systematic_sources: differential sinker volume calibration uncertainty — the volume difference ΔV = V1 − V2 must be known accurately; errors in either V1(T,p) or V2(T,p) propagate into ρ = ΔW/(ΔV · g); this is the dominant systematic source but is smaller than V_sinker uncertainty in the one-sinker method because ΔV is calibrated directly via differential buoyancy in reference fluids

differential adsorption: if fluid adsorption differs between the two sinker materials (quartz vs. silicon, for example), the adsorbed mass does not cancel and introduces a systematic density bias; this effect can reach ~0.005 kg/m³ for polar fluids
temperature measurement uncertainty — bias in PRT calibration propagates through ∂ρ/∂T and the temperature dependence of sinker volumes
pressure measurement uncertainty — bias in pressure transducer propagates through ∂ρ/∂p
residual second-order FTE — if coupling positions are not perfectly identical for the two sinker weighings, a small uncancelled FTE remains; typically < 0.001 kg/m³
gravitational acceleration uncertainty — negligible (< 0.0001%) when g_local is from a gravity survey
uncertainty.operator_dependence: low — the technique is highly automated; operator involvement is mainly in sample preparation, cell loading, and sinker handling; however, improper degassing, differential contamination of the two sinkers, or careless seal installation can compromise the differential cancellation
uncertainty.model_dependence: very low — the differential Archimedes relation ρ = ΔW/(ΔV · g) is exact and model-free; the only model element is the characterization of V1(T,p) and V2(T,p), which relies on well-known elastic and thermal properties of crystalline sinker materials
dominant_error_sources: differential sinker volume calibration ΔV(T,p) (typically 40–60% of the total uncertainty budget)
temperature measurement bias (especially for fluids with large |∂ρ/∂T|)
differential fluid adsorption between the two sinker materials
pressure measurement bias (significant for highly compressible fluids or near the critical point)
reported_as: combined expanded uncertainty U(ρ) at 95% confidence level (k = 2) in kg/m³
relative uncertainty Δρ/ρ in percent or parts per million
individual uncertainty contributions from T, p, ΔV calibration, and differential adsorption listed separately in an uncertainty budget table

description_block.technique_overview: The two-sinker magnetic suspension densimeter is the most accurate method available for measuring the absolute density of fluids over wide ranges of temperature and pressure. It extends the one-sinker magnetic suspension buoyancy technique by employing two sinkers of deliberately different volumes and densities, both immersed in the same sample fluid and weighed sequentially on the same magnetic suspension balance. By taking the differential buoyancy between the two sinkers, all balance-related systematic errors — most critically the force transmission error (FTE) of the magnetic coupling and any zero-point drift — cancel to first order. This method was pioneered by Wagner and Kleinrahm at Ruhr-Universität Bochum and has been adopted by national metrology institutes (NIST, PTB) as the reference technique for primary density standards, routinely achieving combined expanded uncertainties as low as 0.001–0.01 kg/m³ (relative: 0.0001–0.001%).
description_block.how_it_operates: Inside a sealed, pressurized measuring cell, two sinkers rest on separate support cradles when not being weighed. The magnetic suspension coupling, controlled from outside the cell, can selectively lift each sinker to a defined measuring position by switching between three stable coupling positions (zero-point, sinker-1, sinker-2). At each thermodynamic state point (T, p), the measurement cycle proceeds: (1) record the zero-point balance reading with both sinkers on their cradles, (2) engage coupling position 1 to lift sinker 1 and record its apparent weight, (3) return sinker 1 to its cradle, (4) engage coupling position 2 to lift sinker 2 and record its apparent weight. The fluid density is computed from the difference in buoyancy forces on the two sinkers divided by the difference in their volumes, with no need for explicit FTE correction because the coupling force bias is the same for both weighings and cancels in the subtraction.
description_block.core_theory: The two-sinker method is grounded in the differential application of Archimedes' principle. For sinker i (i = 1, 2) of true mass m_i and volume V_i(T,p), the apparent weight in the fluid is W_i = m_i·g − ρ·V_i·g + φ, where φ is the force transmission error of the magnetic coupling (identical for both sinkers at the same coupling position). Subtracting: (W1_vac − W1_fluid) − (W2_vac − W2_fluid) = ρ·g·(V1 − V2), because the coupling error φ cancels. Solving: ρ = [(W1_vac − W1_fluid) − (W2_vac − W2_fluid)] / [(V1(T,p) − V2(T,p))·g]. The sinker materials are chosen so that V1 >> V2 (e.g., quartz glass for sinker 1, silicon for sinker 2) to maximize the denominator (V1 − V2) and hence the measurement sensitivity. Unlike the one-sinker method, the two-sinker result is independent of the absolute accuracy of the balance zero-point, the FTE, and air-side buoyancy corrections.
description_block.setup: The apparatus is arranged vertically with a commercial high-resolution microbalance (1–10 μg readability) at the top, mounted on a vibration-isolated platform inside a draft-free enclosure. Below the balance, the magnetic suspension coupling unit interfaces through a non-magnetic pressure-rated wall (beryllium copper or Hastelloy tube) to the interior of the measuring cell. The cell, typically 100–400 cm³ in volume, houses both sinkers on individual support cradles and is designed for pressures up to 100–300 MPa. A high-stability thermostat jacket (liquid-bath circulation, ±2 mK) surrounds the cell. Calibrated Pt-25 thermometers and a high-accuracy pressure transducer monitor the thermodynamic state. An automated control system sequences the three-position coupling cycle and records all balance, temperature, and pressure data at each state point.
description_block.suitable_for: This technique is the definitive choice when the highest achievable accuracy in fluid density is required — such as for establishing primary reference datasets, calibrating transfer-standard densimeters, and developing or validating high-accuracy equations of state. It is used by NIST, PTB, and leading university laboratories worldwide for benchmark measurements on refrigerants, natural gas components, CO₂ for CCS applications, hydrocarbons, ionic liquids, and aqueous systems. The cancellation of FTE makes it particularly advantageous at high pressures (> 50 MPa) and for low-density gas-phase measurements where the one-sinker FTE correction would approach or exceed the buoyancy signal. It is the method of choice for fluids designated as IUPAC reference standards.
description_block.core_limitations: The two-sinker method requires a larger measuring cell to accommodate both sinkers, increasing sample volume requirements (100–400 cm³) and extending equilibration times. The sequential weighing of two sinkers approximately doubles the measurement time per state point compared to the one-sinker method. The key assumption that FTE cancels exactly requires that both sinkers be weighed at identical coupling conditions; any difference in levitation height introduces a small residual FTE. Differential adsorption between the two sinker materials (e.g., quartz is more adsorptive than silicon for polar molecules) is the most insidious limitation — unlike FTE and balance drift, adsorption does not cancel and can introduce systematic bias of order 0.005 kg/m³ for polar fluids. The technique shares the general limitations of buoyancy densimetry: it cannot measure solids, highly viscous fluids, magnetic fluids, or multiphase systems.
description_block.sample_preparation: Sample preparation follows the same rigorous protocols as the one-sinker method but with additional attention to ensuring both sinkers are equally clean. Samples must be thoroughly degassed by vacuum distillation, freeze-pump-thaw cycles, or prolonged evacuation with stirring to prevent bubble nucleation, which could preferentially attach to one sinker and break the differential cancellation. Mixtures are prepared gravimetrically with composition uncertainty below 0.01 mol%. Particulate matter is removed by sub-micron filtration. Both sinkers and all cell internals are cleaned with a sequence of analytical-grade solvents (acetone, ethanol, n-hexane), dried, and then the cell is evacuated and flushed with clean sample vapor before final filling to remove adsorbed contaminant films.
description_block.calibration_and_references: Calibration requires independent determination of V1(T,p) and V2(T,p) for each sinker by buoyancy measurements in reference fluids of known density. Ultrapure water (IAPWS-95 EOS, uncertainty < 0.001 kg/m³) serves as the primary liquid-phase reference, and high-purity nitrogen (Span et al. 2000 EOS) as the gas-phase reference. The volume difference ΔV(T,p) can also be calibrated directly as a single quantity, which may reduce the combined uncertainty. Sinker masses are determined by vacuum weighing against SI-traceable standards. The FTE cancellation is verified by differential measurements in vacuum — the residual should be zero within balance noise. Temperature sensors are calibrated against ITS-90 fixed points, and the pressure transducer is verified against a dead-weight gauge. A complete validation is performed by measuring a secondary reference fluid (e.g., propane or toluene with established reference EOS) and comparing to literature values within the target uncertainty of 0.003 kg/m³.
description_block.data_interpretation: At each (T, p) state point, the density is computed from the differential Archimedes equation: ρ = [(W1_vac − W1_fluid) − (W2_vac − W2_fluid)] / [(V1(T,p) − V2(T,p)) · g_local]. As an internal consistency check, the individual single-sinker densities ρ_1 and ρ_2 are also computed and compared with the differential result; discrepancies signal adsorption, bubbles, or coupling problems. The ρ(T, p) dataset is fitted to a high-accuracy equation of state (Helmholtz energy formulation, GERG-2008, or modified MBWR) to generate smooth thermodynamic surfaces. Secondary properties — isobaric thermal expansion α_p, isothermal compressibility κ_T, and speed of sound (when combined with Cp) — are obtained by analytical differentiation of the fitted surface. Deviation plots (ρ_exp − ρ_EOS) are standard output to assess both the instrument performance and the quality of existing correlations.
description_block.common_pitfalls: The most frequent pitfall specific to the two-sinker method is differential adsorption: operators may assume that because balance errors cancel, adsorption also cancels, but different sinker materials (quartz vs. silicon) have different surface chemistry and adsorb polar molecules to different extents, producing a persistent systematic bias. Inadequate degassing is equally damaging — even a single microbubble on one sinker, with the other sinker bubble-free, corrupts the differential signal by the full buoyancy of the bubble rather than cancelling as other errors do. Thermal stratification in the large cell, if both sinkers are not at the same temperature, violates the assumption that both sinkers experience identical fluid density. Neglecting to recalibrate sinker volumes after long service periods or after exposure to corrosive samples can degrade accuracy, as surface erosion or deposition changes V differently for the two sinker materials.
description_block.artifacts_and_failure_modes: Differential adsorption is the signature artifact of the two-sinker method: it manifests as a small, pressure-dependent, systematic density offset (typically positive if sinker 1 adsorbs more than sinker 2) that is undetectable without comparison to an independent reference measurement. Asymmetric bubble attachment produces the opposite bias — a spurious density decrease if sinker 1 retains more bubbles than sinker 2. If the coupling mechanism fails to return a sinker cleanly to its cradle, the next sinker weighing inherits a residual force offset, mimicking an FTE that should have cancelled. Seal failure under high pressure causes slow sample loss or air ingress, manifesting as gradual density drift over hours. Physical contact between a sinker and the cell wall or the other sinker interrupts the measurement with erratic balance readings. Quartz-glass sinker 1 is susceptible to microcracking under thermal shock, silently changing its volume and invalidating its calibration.
description_block.reporting_checklist: Publications using the two-sinker magnetic suspension densimeter should report: sinker materials, masses, and volumes with uncertainties, and the method of volume calibration including the reference fluids and equations of state used; explicit statement that the differential (two-sinker) evaluation was employed and that FTE cancels by design; measuring cell material and maximum rated pressure; thermostat type and temperature stability achieved; thermometer type and ITS-90 traceability; pressure transducer model and calibration traceability; sample source, purity, and purification procedure; degassing method; mixture preparation method and composition uncertainty; number of replicate measurement cycles per state point; density data as a function of T and p with combined expanded uncertainties (k = 2, 95% CL); equation of state or correlation used for data fitting; deviation plot versus a reference EOS; discussion of differential adsorption assessment; and validation results against a primary reference fluid. In ThermoML encoding, density values are reported with nCombExpandUncertValue at the 95% confidence level.
